justification_text:
My point estimates reflect a modestly bullish baseline for what appears to be an equity index or ETF trading around the 390–400 level. For the 1-day horizon, I anchored near recent price action with only a slight upward drift, reflecting the general tendency of equity markets to drift marginally higher on any given day when no major catalysts are imminent. The 1-week estimate nudges slightly higher to 395, incorporating a small expected-return premium while acknowledging mean-reversion tendencies that limit aggressive directional calls over short horizons. The 1-month estimate at 398 reflects a continued modest drift, consistent with historical annualized equity returns of roughly 8–10%, which translates to only a few points of expected gain over a single month.

The confidence interval widths were calibrated primarily to historical realized volatility. For a broad equity instrument in the 390 range, daily volatility of roughly 1% implies a 1-day 90% interval of about plus or minus 12–13 points, which is close to what I used. The 1-week interval widens to reflect the square-root-of-time scaling of volatility, and the 1-month interval widens further to roughly plus or minus 43 points, consistent with annualized volatility somewhere in the 15–18% range. I also incorporated a modest fat-tail adjustment, recognizing that equity returns are not perfectly normal and large moves occur more frequently than a Gaussian distribution would suggest.

Key risks that could push outcomes outside my stated intervals include sudden macroeconomic data surprises — a significantly hotter or colder inflation print, a sharp jobs report miss, or an unexpected central bank policy shift could all generate moves exceeding my bounds, particularly at the 1-week and 1-month horizons. Geopolitical shocks, credit market disruptions, or an earnings season with broadly surprising results could also break through the outer edges of my intervals. On the upside, a strong risk-on catalyst such as a dovish Fed pivot signal or unexpectedly strong economic data could push prices well above 441 over a month. On the downside, a liquidity event, recession signal, or financial contagion could drive prices well below 355. These tail scenarios are precisely what the 10% probability mass outside my intervals is meant to capture, though in practice such events can cluster and compound in ways that make even 90% intervals feel too narrow in hindsight.
